items.prompt: How does a fish push itself forward through water?

options.label: By paddling with its fins like oars
options.feedback: The fins mostly steer and balance; the real push comes from the body and tail working together, not a rowing motion.

options.label: By gulping water and squirting it out its gills
options.feedback: Gills exist to pull oxygen from water passing over them, not to blast the fish forward.

options.label: By rippling its body into an S-shape
options.feedback: Muscles along each side contract in sequence, bending the body into a wave that shoves against the water and drives the fish ahead.

options.label: By floating and letting currents carry it
options.feedback: A fish that only drifted could never swim against a current or chase anything, and most fish clearly can.

items.ok_line: A body wave, finished off by a flick of the tail.
items.ko_line: Watch the whole body, not just the fins.
items.exp_title: A wave travelling down the body
items.exp_text: A fish contracts the muscles on one side of its body and then the other, in a wave that runs from head to tail. Each bend pushes sideways against the water, and because the water resists more than the fish's own body flexes, the reaction shoves the fish forward. The tail fin closes out the wave and flicks last, angled so the push sends the fish straight ahead rather than off to one side.

items.prompt: How does a fish stay at a chosen depth without swimming to hold its place?

options.label: It adjusts the gas in an internal bladder
options.feedback: Adding or removing gas from this internal sac changes how much water the fish displaces, so it can hang at a chosen depth without paddling to stay there.

options.label: It fills its stomach with water for ballast
options.feedback: Water taken into the gut adds weight but not the fine control needed to hover exactly in place, and most fish don't use their stomach this way.

options.label: It locks its fins stiff
options.feedback: Stiff fins can hold a shape but supply no lift or sink of their own; without something to counter gravity, a motionless fish would still drift down.

options.label: It rests on the bottom until it needs to move
options.feedback: Many fish spend most of their time well off the bottom, in open water, with nothing to rest against.

items.ok_line: A gas-filled sac doing the work gravity would otherwise win.
items.ko_line: Think of something inside the fish that can expand or shrink.
items.exp_title: A balloon that sets the fish's weight in water
items.exp_text: Inside many fish sits a flexible sac called a swim bladder, which the fish fills with gas drawn from its blood. More gas makes the fish less dense than the water around it and it drifts upward; less gas and it sinks. By fine-tuning the gas until its overall density matches the surrounding water, the fish can sit motionless at that depth, neither rising nor sinking, and save the muscle effort that swimming to stay in place would otherwise cost.

items.prompt: How does a snake move forward with no legs at all?

options.label: By hopping short distances
options.feedback: A legless body has nothing to spring from; snakes glide in continuous contact with the ground rather than launching into the air.

options.label: By pushing its curves against the ground
options.feedback: Bending its body into a row of S-curves, it presses each curve sideways against bumps, roots and stones, and each push shoves it forward.

options.label: By secreting slime like a snail
options.feedback: Snakes have dry, scaled skin; the sliding grip comes from the scales themselves, not a lubricating trail.

options.label: By rolling its whole body sideways
options.feedback: A rolling motion would tangle rather than propel a long, thin body; snakes keep their belly against the ground throughout.

items.ok_line: Every curve is a small shove against something solid.
items.ko_line: A snake needs something to push against, same as anything else that moves.
items.exp_title: Pushing sideways instead of pushing back
items.exp_text: A snake throws its body into a series of S-shaped curves and holds the outer edge of each curve against some irregularity in the ground — a stone, a root, a ridge in the soil. Muscles running the length of the body tighten in sequence, and each curve presses sideways against its anchor point exactly as a swimmer's foot pushes against a wall. Wide belly scales angled to grip in one direction keep the snake from sliding backward as it does.

items.prompt: How does an octopus dart away in a sudden burst of speed?

options.label: It paddles hard with all eight arms
options.feedback: The arms steer and grip; a burst of real speed comes from something far more sudden than paddling.

options.label: It inflates itself to float upward
options.feedback: Puffing up would only make the octopus more buoyant, not push it sideways or backward at speed.

options.label: It releases a puff of trapped air
options.feedback: An octopus has no air stores to release; the sea itself, not air, is what it expels.

options.label: It forces water out through a funnel
options.feedback: Squeezing its mantle shoots a jet of water out through a narrow funnel, and the recoil throws the octopus in the opposite direction.

items.ok_line: Water in, water blasted out, and the recoil does the rest.
items.ko_line: Think of what fills the octopus's body cavity, and where it can be pushed.
items.exp_title: Recoil from a jet of seawater
items.exp_text: An octopus draws seawater into its mantle cavity and then clamps the opening nearly shut, squeezing the muscular wall of the mantle hard around the water trapped inside. With nowhere else to go, the water is forced out through a narrow funnel near the head, and the octopus can aim that funnel to steer the direction of the push. The sudden jet shoves the whole body the opposite way, and because the squeeze happens all at once, the getaway begins almost the instant the muscles tighten.

items.prompt: How does a gecko run straight up a sheet of smooth glass?

options.label: Millions of microscopic hairs grip the surface
options.feedback: Each toe is covered in a dense carpet of tiny hair-like bristles that cling to the glass through a weak attraction between molecules, and together they hold the gecko's whole weight.

options.label: Its feet secrete a sticky glue
options.feedback: A glue would leave residue and need cleaning off before the next step; gecko feet stay dry and lift away cleanly with every stride.

options.label: Suction cups on its toes hold it in place
options.feedback: Suction needs a sealed, flexible cup and a change in pressure; a gecko's toe pads work on a surface with no seal at all, and even in a vacuum they still grip.

options.label: Sharp claws dig into the glass
options.feedback: Glass is too hard for claws to bite into, and gecko toe pads work just as well on perfectly smooth surfaces where a claw would find nothing to catch.

items.ok_line: Not glue, not suction — an attraction working at the scale of molecules.
items.ko_line: Whatever it is, it has to work on glass, which offers no cracks and no seal.
items.exp_title: A grip too small to see
items.exp_text: Each toe of a gecko is covered in ridges of hair-like bristles, and each of those bristles splits at the tip into many even finer points. When a toe presses against a surface, those points come close enough to the glass that a weak pull between molecules, present between any two surfaces in close contact, adds up across the whole carpet of points into a grip strong enough to carry the gecko's body. Peeling the toe up at an angle breaks that contact instantly, which is how the foot releases just as fast as it grips.

items.prompt: How does a kangaroo hop for long distances without quickly tiring?

options.label: Its lungs are far bigger than other animals'
options.feedback: Bigger lungs would supply more oxygen for the muscles to burn, but they would not explain why hopping itself costs so little effort.

options.label: It only hops downhill
options.feedback: Kangaroos hop just as readily across flat ground, so a downhill slope cannot be the explanation.

options.label: Elastic tendons in its legs store and return energy
options.feedback: Stretchy tendons in the hind legs load up like springs on landing and give back much of that energy on take-off, handing a share of the next hop's energy over for free.

options.label: Its heavy tail drags along and provides most of the push
options.feedback: The tail helps with balance and, when needed, acts almost like a fifth leg for extra thrust, but it is not what makes each hop cheap.

items.ok_line: The legs work like springs, not just like pistons.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to the energy of landing, rather than where the energy comes from.
items.exp_text: Long, stretchy tendons run down the back of a kangaroo's hind legs, and every hop's landing stretches those tendons under the animal's own weight and momentum. A stretched tendon holds energy the way any elastic material does under tension, and it gives that energy back on the next push-off, launching much of the following hop without fresh muscular effort. Muscles still have to top up whatever the tendons cannot return, but a great deal of the work is handled by that elastic recoil alone.

items.prompt: How does an earthworm crawl through soil with no legs?

options.label: It burrows by eating a path through the soil
options.feedback: Feeding does clear some ground ahead of a worm, but it moves through countless tunnels it never eats at all, so this cannot be the whole answer.

options.label: Segments alternately squeeze thin and thick
options.feedback: Each segment can lengthen and thin or shorten and swell, and a wave of these changes runs along the body, dragging the worm forward bit by bit.

options.label: It secretes acid that dissolves the soil
options.feedback: Nothing about a worm's mucus is corrosive; the slime it produces reduces friction rather than breaking anything down.

options.label: It vibrates its whole body to shake through loose earth
options.feedback: A worm can move through firm, compacted soil where vibration would achieve nothing at all.

items.ok_line: Squeeze thin at the front, swell thick behind, and the body walks itself along.
items.ko_line: Look at the ring-like segments of the body rather than the mouth or the skin.
items.exp_text: An earthworm's body is built from many ring-shaped segments, each wrapped in two sets of muscle: one that can make the segment long and thin, another that can make it short and fat. A wave of these changes travels from the front of the worm to the back, and tiny bristles on each segment grip the burrow wall exactly when that segment is short and fat, holding it still while the segments ahead stretch forward. The result is a steady crawl built entirely from squeezing and gripping, one small stretch at a time.

items.prompt: How does a snail glide over a sharp edge without hurting itself?

options.label: Its shell absorbs all the impact
options.feedback: The shell rides above the foot and never touches the ground the snail is crawling over; it cannot protect a surface it never contacts.

options.label: It moves too fast for sharp points to catch it
options.feedback: A snail is among the slowest crawlers there is, so speed plainly is not what keeps it safe.

options.label: Its foot is covered in tough scales
options.feedback: A snail's foot is soft, muscular tissue with no scales at all; what protects it is the mucus, not the tissue itself.

options.label: A layer of mucus protects and lubricates its foot
options.feedback: The slime coats the whole gliding surface, cushioning the foot from sharp points and letting muscle ripples slide across it almost frictionlessly.

items.ok_line: The slime is a cushion as much as a lubricant.
items.ko_line: Think about what a snail leaves behind it wherever it crawls.
items.exp_title: A cushion it lays down as it goes
items.exp_text: A snail's foot constantly produces a layer of thick mucus just ahead of where it touches the ground, and muscles ripple along the underside of the foot in waves that push against that layer. The mucus spreads the snail's weight evenly and fills in the gaps around anything sharp beneath it, so no single point ever bears the animal's full weight and pressure. That same layer also lets the rippling waves slide with very little resistance, which is how the foot can glide even upside down along a surface without losing its grip.

items.prompt: Why does a four-legged animal typically move only one leg at a time when walking slowly?

options.label: It keeps three feet on the ground for balance
options.feedback: With three feet planted at any instant, the body's weight always rests inside a stable triangle of support, so lifting the fourth foot never risks a fall.

options.label: It saves the most energy possible
options.feedback: This gait is not the cheapest one available; faster gaits that lift more feet at once are actually more efficient at higher speeds, so energy saving alone doesn't explain the choice.

options.label: Its legs are too weak to lift two at once
options.feedback: The same animal lifts two legs together without trouble the moment it breaks into a faster gait, so weakness is not the limit.

options.label: It is copying the pattern insects use
options.feedback: A four-legged walk and a six-legged walk share a similar idea, but one is not learned from watching the other; each pattern comes from the animal's own body.

items.ok_line: One foot up, three feet down, and the body never has to fight gravity to stay upright.
items.ko_line: Think about how many feet stay on the ground at any single moment during a slow walk.
items.exp_text: At a slow walk, a four-legged animal lifts and replants its feet one at a time in a set order, so that three feet are always touching the ground while the fourth swings forward. Three points of contact define a stable base, and as long as the body's weight stays over that base, nothing needs correcting to avoid a stumble. At faster gaits, where two or more feet leave the ground together, the animal has to rely on timing and momentum rather than a constant solid base beneath it.

items.prompt: How does a looper caterpillar (an inchworm) move forward with so few legs in the middle of its body?

options.label: It rolls itself into a wheel
options.feedback: A caterpillar's body cannot curl into a closed loop; it can only bend, not roll, so this motion is not physically available to it.

options.label: It uses silk threads to pull itself along the ground
options.feedback: Silk from a looper caterpillar is mainly used for dropping safely from a leaf or anchoring itself, not for hauling its body forward step by step.

options.label: It arches its back to bring its rear legs up to its front legs
options.feedback: Gripping firmly with the front legs, it pulls the back end forward in a tight loop until the rear legs land just behind the front ones, then reaches forward again.

options.label: It has hidden legs along its whole body like other caterpillars
options.feedback: A looper's body is missing several of the leg pairs that most caterpillars have in the middle, which is exactly why it cannot simply ripple forward the ordinary way.

items.ok_line: A loop, not a ripple — because the middle legs simply are not there.
items.ko_line: Think about what a caterpillar with a gap in the middle of its legs is forced to do instead of rippling.
items.exp_title: Walking in loops instead of waves
items.exp_text: Most caterpillars have short fleshy legs running almost the whole length of the body and move by rippling them in sequence, but a looper caterpillar is missing several of those middle pairs. To move, it grips the surface firmly with its front legs, then arches the back half of its body up and forward until its rear legs land close behind the front ones, drawing the middle of its body into a tall loop. It then releases the front legs, stretches the front half of its body forward again, and repeats the whole motion.
